claim: Residual force enhancement (rFE) is a history-dependent property of skeletal muscle defined as the enhanced isometric force following active muscle lengthening relative to the isometric force obtained during a fixed-end reference contraction at the same muscle length and level of activation.
source: Residual force enhancement (rFE) is a history-dependent property of skeletal muscle and is defined as the enhanced isometric (i.e. steady-state) force following active muscle lengthening (i.e. stretch) relative to the isometric force obtained during a fixed-end reference contraction at the same muscle length and level of activation (Cook and McDonagh, 1995; Edman et al., 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cook and McDonagh, 1995 and Edman et al., 1978, which are referenced works that established this definition.

claim: rFE has been observed across muscle structural scales ranging from single sarcomeres to isolated fibres from animals and humans to whole human muscles working in vivo during artificially evoked and voluntary contractions.
source: rFE has been observed across muscle structural scales ranging from single sarcomeres (Leonard et al., 2010) to isolated fibres from animals (Abbott and Aubert, 1952) and humans (Pinnell et al., 2019) to whole human muscles working in vivo (Cook and McDonagh, 1995) during artificially evoked and voluntary contractions (Lee and Herzog, 2002; Seiberl et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies that observed rFE at different structural scales: Leonard et al., 2010 for sarcomeres, Abbott and Aubert, 1952 for animal fibres, Pinnell et al., 2019 for human fibres, Cook and McDonagh, 1995 for whole muscles, and Lee and Herzog, 2002 and Seiberl et al., 2015 for different contraction types.

claim: In vitro and in situ experiments have shown that rFE is independent of stretch velocity.
source: In vitro and in situ experiments have shown that rFE is independent of stretch velocity (Edman et al., 1978; Tilp et al., 2009), but dependent on muscle length, whereby rFE is greater when the stretch ends at longer muscle lengths (Bullimore et al., 2007; Hisey et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Edman et al., 1978 and Tilp et al., 2009, which are studies that demonstrated rFE independence from stretch velocity.

claim: rFE is dependent on muscle length, whereby rFE is greater when the stretch ends at longer muscle lengths.
source: In vitro and in situ experiments have shown that rFE is independent of stretch velocity (Edman et al., 1978; Tilp et al., 2009), but dependent on muscle length, whereby rFE is greater when the stretch ends at longer muscle lengths (Bullimore et al., 2007; Hisey et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bullimore et al., 2007 and Hisey et al., 2009, which are studies that demonstrated the muscle length dependence of rFE.

claim: rFE generally increases with increasing stretch amplitude until some critical amplitude on the descending limb of the force-length relationship.
source: rFE generally increases with increasing stretch amplitude (Edman et al., 1982; Edman et al., 1978) until some critical amplitude on the descending limb of the force-length relationship (Bullimore et al., 2007; Hisey et al., 2009), but increasing stretch amplitude does not necessarily increase rFE when the stretch ends at shorter muscle lengths (Hisey et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Edman et al., 1982, Edman et al., 1978, Bullimore et al., 2007, and Hisey et al., 2009, which are studies that examined the relationship between stretch amplitude and rFE.

claim: Increasing stretch amplitude does not necessarily increase rFE when the stretch ends at shorter muscle lengths.
source: rFE generally increases with increasing stretch amplitude (Edman et al., 1982; Edman et al., 1978) until some critical amplitude on the descending limb of the force-length relationship (Bullimore et al., 2007; Hisey et al., 2009), but increasing stretch amplitude does not necessarily increase rFE when the stretch ends at shorter muscle lengths (Hisey et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hisey et al., 2009, which demonstrated that stretch amplitude does not always increase rFE at shorter muscle lengths.

claim: A recent meta-analysis concluded that rFE estimated from measured net joint torques was not dependent on stretch amplitude during artificially evoked or voluntary contractions.
source: In a recent meta-analysis, de Campos et al., 2022 analysed how stretch amplitude affects in vivo rFE and concluded that rFE, which was estimated from measured net joint torques, was not dependent on stretch amplitude (i.e. the amount of joint rotation) during artificially evoked or voluntary contractions.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Campos et al., 2022, which is a meta-analysis that examined the relationship between stretch amplitude and in vivo rFE.

claim: Power et al., 2013 showed that rFE occurs at both short and long muscle lengths.
source: Power et al., 2013 showed that rFE occurs at both short and long muscle lengths, whereas other studies found rFE only at long muscle lengths (Bakenecker et al., 2020; Fukutani et al., 2017; Shim and Garner, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Power et al., 2013, which is a study that observed rFE at both short and long muscle lengths.

claim: Other studies found rFE only at long muscle lengths.
source: Power et al., 2013 showed that rFE occurs at both short and long muscle lengths, whereas other studies found rFE only at long muscle lengths (Bakenecker et al., 2020; Fukutani et al., 2017; Shim and Garner, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bakenecker et al., 2020, Fukutani et al., 2017, and Shim and Garner, 2012, which are studies that observed rFE only at long muscle lengths.

claim: Martin et al., 2018 showed that the shear-wave propagation velocity in free tendons depends primarily on axial stress under physiological loads.
source: These authors previously showed that the shear-wave propagation velocity in free tendons depends primarily on axial stress under physiological loads, and that in vivo tendon shear-wave speeds can be tracked by a shear-wave tensiometer, which consists of a skin-mounted tapping device and two miniature accelerometers.
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to Martin et al., 2018, which is a study that demonstrated the relationship between shear-wave propagation velocity and axial stress in tendons.

claim: Squared tendon shear-wave speeds measured with a shear-wave tensiometer strongly correlate with joint torques during fixed-end knee extension and plantar flexion contractions.
source: The squared tendon shear-wave speeds measured with this device were shown to strongly correlate with joint torques during fixed-end knee extension and plantar flexion contractions (Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Martin et al., 2018, which demonstrated the strong correlation between squared shear-wave speeds and joint torques.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Martin et al., 2018, which demonstrated the correlation between squared shear-wave speeds and joint torques during gait.

claim: The greatest rFE was found at the very long muscle length for both rFETQ and rFEWS measures.
source: For both rFETQ and rFEWS measures, we found the greatest rFE at the very long muscle length.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the highest rFE values at the very long muscle length.

claim: In vivo rFE is maximised during submaximal voluntary contractions of the human quadriceps at a very long muscle length.
source: Taken together, rFETQ and rFEWS findings indicate that in vivo rFE is maximised during submaximal voluntary contractions of the human quadriceps at a very long muscle length, and that in vivo rFE is more strongly correlated with VL muscle fascicle length than fascicle stretch amplitude.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing greatest rFE at very long muscle length.

claim: In vivo rFE is more strongly correlated with VL muscle fascicle length than fascicle stretch amplitude.
source: Taken together, rFETQ and rFEWS findings indicate that in vivo rFE is maximised during submaximal voluntary contractions of the human quadriceps at a very long muscle length, and that in vivo rFE is more strongly correlated with VL muscle fascicle length than fascicle stretch amplitude.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the correlation analysis showing significant relationships with fascicle length but not stretch amplitude.

claim: The findings are in accordance with a previous study by Bakenecker et al., 2020 that found significant rFE only at a long (10.7±5.5%), but not at a short (1.3±3.1%) muscle length.
source: This is in accordance with a previous study with a similar setup, where we also found significant rFE only at a long (10.7±5.5%), but not at a short (1.3±3.1%) muscle length (Bakenecker et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited previous work by Bakenecker et al., 2020.

claim: Similar findings have been reported by Shim and Garner, 2012 at short (no rFE) and long (4.7%) quadriceps' muscle lengths.
source: Similar findings have been reported by Shim and Garner, 2012 at short (no rFE) and long (4.7%) quadriceps' muscle lengths.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shim and Garner, 2012, which reported similar findings.

claim: Power et al., 2013 tested at 60° knee flexion for their short muscle length condition, which would result in a longer muscle length and therefore significant rFE based on the current study's data.
source: Unlike the aforementioned studies, which either tested at a common knee flexion angle of 40° knee flexion or confirmed that the short muscle length was situated on the ascending limb of the quadriceps' torque-angle relationship, Power et al., 2013 tested at 60° knee flexion for their short muscle length condition, which would result in a longer muscle length and therefore significant rFE based on our data (Figures 1 and 3).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the current study's findings with the methodology of Power et al., 2013.

claim: Bullimore et al., 2007 showed that rFE increases with increasing stretch amplitude until a critical amplitude (9 mm of stretch) when the stretch ends on the descending limb of the force-length relationship.
source: For example, Bullimore et al., 2007 showed that rFE increases with increasing stretch amplitude until a critical amplitude (9 mm of stretch) when the stretch ends on the descending limb of the force-length relationship.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bullimore et al., 2007, which demonstrated this relationship.

claim: Hisey et al., 2009 showed that rFE only increases with increasing stretch amplitude until a critical amplitude (12 mm of stretch) when the stretch ends at very long muscle fascicle lengths on the descending limb of the force-length relationship.
source: Hisey et al., 2009 later showed that rFE only increases with increasing stretch amplitude until a critical amplitude (12 mm of stretch) when the stretch ends at very long muscle fascicle lengths on the descending limb of the force-length relationship (i.e. 9 mm longer than the optimum length).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hisey et al., 2009, which demonstrated this relationship.

claim: It is unlikely that greater stretch amplitudes contributed to greater rFE at the long and very long muscle lengths compared with the short muscle length.
source: As we observed no significant repeated-measures linear relationship between VL fascicle stretch amplitude and rFETQ (Figure 2), it is unlikely that greater stretch amplitudes contributed to greater rFE at the long and very long muscle lengths compared with the short muscle length.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of significant correlation between stretch amplitude and rFE.

claim: Based on the findings of Hisey et al., 2009, it is unlikely that greater stretch amplitudes to the short muscle length would have changed the rFE values observed.
source: Based on the findings of Hisey et al., 2009, where increasing stretch amplitude did not increase the amount of rFE at a target muscle length 3 mm shorter than the muscle's optimal length for maximum isometric force production, it is further unlikely that greater stretch amplitudes to the short muscle length (i.e. on the ascending limb of the force-length relationship) would have changed the rFE values we observed.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings of Hisey et al., 2009 applied to the current study's context.

claim: The increase in rFE with muscle length could potentially be due to a greater increase in stiffness of a passive elastic structure, such as titin, as it is stretched to longer lengths.
source: The increase in rFE with muscle length could potentially be due to a greater increase in stiffness of a passive elastic structure, such as titin (Rassier and Herzog, 2005), as it is stretched to longer lengths.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on a proposed mechanism cited from Rassier and Herzog, 2005.

claim: rFE magnitudes based on corrected knee extension torques of 2±5%, 7±5%, and 12±8% at the short, long, and very long muscle lengths are in accordance with findings from Seiberl et al., 2012.
source: In this study, we found rFE magnitudes based on corrected knee extension torques of 2±5%, 7±5%, and 12±8% at the short, long, and very long muscle lengths, respectively. Based on PT shear-wave-speed measures, we observed rFE magnitudes of 8±12%, 6±10%, and 38±27% at the same respective lengths. Except for the rFEWS values at the very long muscle length, the rFE values from this study are in accordance with findings from the study of Seiberl et al., 2012, which also had participants perform submaximal voluntary stretch-hold and fixed-end reference contractions of the human quadriceps.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited work by Seiberl et al., 2012.

claim: At a similar crank-arm angle (100° knee flexion) compared with the very long muscle length condition (104±6°), Seiberl et al., 2012 observed rFE magnitudes of 7–11% and 3–5% at 30% and 60% of the maximum voluntary activity level, respectively.
source: At a similar crank-arm angle (100° knee flexion) compared with what we used for the very long muscle length condition (104±6°), Seiberl et al., 2012 observed rFE magnitudes of 7–11% and 3–5% at 30% and 60% of the maximum voluntary activity level, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Seiberl et al., 2012, which reported these rFE magnitudes.

claim: Other studies that investigated the human plantar flexors and the adductor pollicis showed similar rFE magnitudes (7–13%) during submaximal voluntary stretch-hold contractions.
source: Other studies that investigated the human plantar flexors and the adductor pollicis showed similar rFE magnitudes (7–13%) during submaximal voluntary stretch-hold contractions (Oskouei and Herzog, 2006; Oskouei and Herzog, 2005; Pinniger and Cresswell, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oskouei and Herzog, 2006, Oskouei and Herzog, 2005, and Pinniger and Cresswell, 2007.

claim: rFE magnitudes greater than ~15% have only been found for electrically stimulated human muscles.
source: rFE magnitudes greater than ~15% have only been found for electrically stimulated human muscles (Cook and McDonagh, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cook and McDonagh, 1995.

claim: The rFEWS values above 25% calculated in this study might be erroneous.
source: The rFEWS values above 25% (see Figure 1B) we calculated might therefore be erroneous, which is supported by the much lower than expected normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds determined during the fixed-end reference contractions at the very long muscle length (see Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the unexpectedly high rFEWS values and comparison with literature values.

claim: The average agreement between normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds and estimated PT forces was 62% at the very long muscle length compared with 86% and 91% at the short and long muscle lengths, respectively.
source: Unsurprisingly, the average agreement between normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds and estimated PT forces was worst at this muscle length at 62% compared with 86% and 91% at the short and long muscle lengths, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing shear-wave speeds and estimated forces.

claim: The accuracy of the shear-wave-speed estimates, or PT force estimates, might decrease as the PT's orientation changes relative to the tibia's long axis.
source: This might be because the accuracy of the shear-wave-speed estimates, or PT force estimates, decreases as the PT's orientation changes relative to the tibia's long axis (Draganich et al., 1987), however this deserves further research.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on a cited mechanism from Draganich et al., 1987.

claim: Obtaining plausible shear-wave speeds from the PT proved to be very difficult.
source: In general, obtaining plausible shear-wave speeds from the PT proved to be very difficult.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental experience described in the Discussion section.

claim: Martin et al., 2018 could not calculate shear-wave speeds from the PT during parts of the gait cycle.
source: In some of our participants (n=5), the shear-wave tensiometry technique resulted in unusable data, which is not that surprising, considering that Martin et al., 2018 also could not calculate shear-wave speeds from the PT during parts of the gait cycle (see their Supplementary Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2018, which reported similar difficulties.

claim: An average agreement between squared PT shear-wave speeds and estimated PT forces above 90% was found for only four participants.
source: For the remaining participants in the current study whose shear-wave speeds could be quantified, the accuracy of the measurements across different knee joint angles is questionable considering that we found an average agreement between squared PT shear-wave speeds and estimated PT forces above 90% for four participants only (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PT shear-wave-speed measurements became implausible during passive conditions where the MTU was at rest, during active conditions with stretch under high tension, and during maximal voluntary contractions.
source: PT shear-wave-speed measurements also became implausible during passive conditions where the MTU was at rest, during active conditions with stretch under high tension (Figure 4B), and during maximal voluntary contractions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the Discussion and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Squared shear-wave speeds changed drastically across different joint angles, despite similar torque levels.
source: Further, squared shear-wave speeds changed drastically across different joint angles, despite similar torque levels (Figure 4B/E and C/F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B/E and C/F.

claim: Quantifying PT loads can be problematic with shear-wave tensiometry and the PT shear-wave speeds estimated by this technique might be inaccurate.
source: Taken together, this indicates that quantifying PT loads can be problematic with shear-wave tensiometry and that the PT shear-wave speeds estimated by this technique might be inaccurate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the various problems observed with shear-wave tensiometry measurements.

claim: The main assumption of shear-wave tensiometry is that the shear-wave propagation speed depends primarily on tendon axial stress under physiological loads.
source: The main assumption of shear-wave tensiometry is that the shear-wave propagation speed depends primarily on tendon axial stress under physiological loads (Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2018, which established this assumption.

claim: This assumption might not hold true under very low or high physiological loads.
source: Even if this assumption holds true, which might not be the case under very low or high physiological loads (Blank et al., 2022; Sarvazyan et al., 2013), axial stress is influenced by both the force in the tendon and the tendon's architecture (i.e. the width and thickness of the tendon).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blank et al., 2022 and Sarvazyan et al., 2013, which suggest limitations to the assumption.

claim: Axial stress is influenced by both the force in the tendon and the tendon's architecture.
source: Even if this assumption holds true, which might not be the case under very low or high physiological loads (Blank et al., 2022; Sarvazyan et al., 2013), axial stress is influenced by both the force in the tendon and the tendon's architecture (i.e. the width and thickness of the tendon).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the relationship between stress, force, and cross-sectional area.

claim: Martin et al., 2020 suggests that the calibration gain required to estimate tendon stress based on tendon shear-wave speed appears to increase with increasing tendon aspect ratios.
source: A recent study by Martin et al., 2020 suggests that the calibration gain required to estimate tendon stress based on tendon shear-wave speed appears to increase with increasing tendon aspect ratios (i.e. increasing tendon width relative to tendon thickness).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2020, which reported this relationship.

claim: When the tendon's architecture changes under different contraction conditions, shear-wave speeds could vary at the same tendon stress.
source: Accordingly, when the tendon's architecture changes (e.g. through deformation of the tendon due to an applied stress) (Kuervers et al., 2021) under different contraction conditions (e.g. during a stretch-hold contraction that covers different joint angles and contraction intensities), shear-wave speeds could vary at the same tendon stress.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the relationship between tendon architecture and shear-wave speed, with citation to Kuervers et al., 2021.

claim: Shear-wave speeds may not accurately reflect tendon stress unless the changes in tendon architecture are accounted for.
source: Thus, shear-wave speeds may not accurately reflect tendon stress unless the changes in tendon architecture are accounted for.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the discussion about tendon architecture changes affecting shear-wave speeds.

claim: In former studies, high correlations between squared shear-wave speed and torque measures were found when muscle activities and corresponding tendon stresses were low during preferred-speed walking.
source: In former studies (Keuler et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2018), high correlations between squared shear-wave speed (≤80 m2 s–2) and torque measures (≤200 Nm) were found when muscle activities and corresponding tendon stresses were low during preferred-speed walking (≤50 MPa).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Keuler et al., 2019 and Martin et al., 2018, which reported these correlations.

claim: Under higher knee extension torques and presumably higher tendon stresses at submaximal muscle activity levels, the estimated PT force-angle relationships were not reflected by the squared shear-wave-speed measures.
source: In contrast, under the higher knee extension torques (112–296 Nm) and presumably higher tendon stresses (>50 MPa) at the submaximal muscle activity levels that were used in this study, the estimated PT force-angle relationships were not reflected by the squared shear-wave-speed measures (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Squared shear-wave-speed estimates were unreasonably high when participants increased their activation level during the maximal voluntary contractions.
source: Additionally, squared shear-wave-speed estimates were unreasonably high when participants increased their activation level during the maximal voluntary contractions in the first part of the experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: High tendon stresses and changing tendon dimensions might be problematic for accurately estimating PT tendon loads based on shear-wave-speed measures.
source: Therefore, high tendon stresses and changing tendon dimensions might be problematic for accurately estimating PT tendon loads based on shear-wave-speed measures.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed problems with shear-wave speed measurements at high loads.

claim: Estimates of PT shear-wave speeds might be affected by differences in subcutaneous tissue thickness between individuals.
source: Estimates of PT shear-wave speeds might additionally be affected by differences in subcutaneous tissue thickness between individuals as Martin et al., 2018 showed that the propagating shear wave within the deep tendon was not identical to the shear wave propagating along the skin.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on a cited observation from Martin et al., 2018.

claim: Compared with the Achilles tendon, the PT has more overlying subcutaneous tissue and is smaller in thickness in its mid-region.
source: Compared with the Achilles tendon, the PT has more overlying subcutaneous tissue (Bravo-Sánchez et al., 2019) and is smaller in thickness in its mid-region (Coombes et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bravo-Sánchez et al., 2019 and Coombes et al., 2018.

claim: Thicker subcutaneous tissue over a thinner tendon might result in poorer shear-wave propagation within the PT compared with the Achilles tendon and less accurate shear-wave-speed estimates.
source: These factors might result in poorer shear-wave propagation within the PT compared with the Achilles tendon and less accurate shear-wave-speed estimates.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from anatomical differences between tendons.

claim: Previous in vivo experiments that examined rFE during voluntary contractions have identified a number of participants not showing rFE, called non-responders.
source: Previous in vivo experiments that examined rFE during voluntary contractions have identified a number of participants not showing rFE (Hahn et al., 2012; Hahn et al., 2007; Oskouei and Herzog, 2006; Tilp et al., 2009). These participants were subsequently called non-responders.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2012, Hahn et al., 2007, Oskouei and Herzog, 2006, and Tilp et al., 2009.

claim: There was no participant in the current study's dataset who consistently showed no rFE across the three muscle lengths tested.
source: However, in opposition to the idea of there being a true non-responder, there was no participant in our dataset who consistently showed no rFE across the three muscle lengths we tested.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study.

claim: There is no true non-responder to rFE.
source: We thus speculate there is no true non-responder.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on the observation that no participant consistently showed no rFE.

claim: Paternoster et al., 2021 showed that voluntary rFE appeared inconsistently in the same participants across five testing sessions, whereas during submaximal tetanic electrical muscle stimulation, all participants consistently showed rFE.
source: This speculation is supported by recent work by Paternoster et al., 2021, who showed that voluntary rFE appeared inconsistently in the same participants across five testing sessions, whereas during submaximal tetanic electrical muscle stimulation, all participants consistently showed rFE.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Paternoster et al., 2021, which reported these findings.

claim: Having participants match muscle activity levels through voluntary effort, rather than through artificial stimulation, likely adds variability to rFE estimates and might contribute to the 'non-responder' phenomenon.
source: Indeed, having participants match muscle activity levels through voluntary effort, rather than through artificial stimulation, likely adds variability to rFE estimates (especially over a short duration analysis window like the one used here), and might contribute to the 'non-responder' phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison between voluntary and electrically stimulated contractions.

claim: rFE values could be influenced by different preloads prior to the stretch phase of the stretch-hold contractions at the short, long, and very long muscle lengths.
source: Although we performed feedback-controlled contractions based on EMG recordings to ensure the same level of superficial quadriceps' activity during stretch-hold and fixed-end reference contractions and we assessed VL muscle fascicle stretch magnitudes, our rFE values could be influenced by different preloads prior to the stretch phase of the stretch-hold contractions at the short, long, and very long muscle lengths.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a potential limitation of the study based on the experimental design.

claim: Using a preload prior to a stretch-hold contraction at the MTU level results in shortening-isometric-stretch-isometric muscle fascicle behavior, where the initial shortening of muscle fascicles increases with an increasing preload or a shorter initial muscle length.
source: Due to the relatively high compliance of human lower limb MTUs, using a preload prior to a stretch-hold contraction at the MTU level results in shortening-isometric-stretch-isometric muscle fascicle behavior, where the initial shortening of muscle fascicles increases with an increasing preload or a shorter initial muscle length.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the behavior of compliant MTUs during contractions.

claim: rFE can be influenced by the amount of shortening preceding stretch.
source: As rFE can be influenced by the amount of shortening preceding stretch (Lee et al., 2001) and active shortening can induce residual force depression (i.e. a reduction in the steady-state force following shortening Abbott and Aubert, 1952; Granzier et al., 1989), differences in muscle fascicle shortening across the three tested muscle lengths could have influenced the estimated rFE magnitudes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2001, Abbott and Aubert, 1952, and Granzier et al., 1989.

claim: Active shortening can induce residual force depression.
source: As rFE can be influenced by the amount of shortening preceding stretch (Lee et al., 2001) and active shortening can induce residual force depression (i.e. a reduction in the steady-state force following shortening Abbott and Aubert, 1952; Granzier et al., 1989), differences in muscle fascicle shortening across the three tested muscle lengths could have influenced the estimated rFE magnitudes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abbott and Aubert, 1952 and Granzier et al., 1989.

claim: Differences in muscle fascicle shortening across the three tested muscle lengths could have influenced the estimated rFE magnitudes.
source: As rFE can be influenced by the amount of shortening preceding stretch (Lee et al., 2001) and active shortening can induce residual force depression (i.e. a reduction in the steady-state force following shortening Abbott and Aubert, 1952; Granzier et al., 1989), differences in muscle fascicle shortening across the three tested muscle lengths could have influenced the estimated rFE magnitudes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited literature about shortening effects on force.

claim: Stretch amplitudes and muscle fascicle lengths were assessed from only a limited region within the VL muscle.
source: Further, we only assessed stretch amplitudes and muscle fascicle lengths from a limited region within the VL muscle and we needed to perform linear extrapolation to estimate fascicle lengths, so we recommend that future studies investigate a muscle with shorter and less curved fascicles to better evaluate the influence of stretch amplitude and fascicle length on rFE.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the study's methodology.

claim: Linear extrapolation was needed to estimate fascicle lengths.
source: Further, we only assessed stretch amplitudes and muscle fascicle lengths from a limited region within the VL muscle and we needed to perform linear extrapolation to estimate fascicle lengths, so we recommend that future studies investigate a muscle with shorter and less curved fascicles to better evaluate the influence of stretch amplitude and fascicle length on rFE.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a methodological limitation of the study.

claim: Future studies should investigate a muscle with shorter and less curved fascicles to better evaluate the influence of stretch amplitude and fascicle length on rFE.
source: Further, we only assessed stretch amplitudes and muscle fascicle lengths from a limited region within the VL muscle and we needed to perform linear extrapolation to estimate fascicle lengths, so we recommend that future studies investigate a muscle with shorter and less curved fascicles to better evaluate the influence of stretch amplitude and fascicle length on rFE.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the limitations identified in the current study.

claim: Assessing PT loads with shear-wave tensiometry might be inaccurate based on the low agreement (<90%) across tested muscle lengths between normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds and normalised PT forces estimated from corrected knee extension torques.
source: Additionally, the low agreement (<90%) across tested muscle lengths between normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds and normalised PT forces estimated from corrected knee extension torques suggests that assessing PT loads with shear-wave tensiometry might be inaccurate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing poor agreement between the two measurement methods.

claim: Sixteen healthy males participated in the study initially.
source: Sixteen healthy males (age 27.9±5.3 years; height 186.3±5.6 cm; weight 83.4±8.6 kg) gave free written informed consent prior to participating in the study, 11 of whom (age 28.4±5.9 years; height 187.1±5.8 cm; weight 82.8±8.0 kg) had data that could be analysed as their PT shear-wave speeds could be calculated.
evidence: The claim is supported by participant demographic data presented in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Eleven participants had data that could be analysed as their PT shear-wave speeds could be calculated.
source: Sixteen healthy males (age 27.9±5.3 years; height 186.3±5.6 cm; weight 83.4±8.6 kg) gave free written informed consent prior to participating in the study, 11 of whom (age 28.4±5.9 years; height 187.1±5.8 cm; weight 82.8±8.0 kg) had data that could be analysed as their PT shear-wave speeds could be calculated.
evidence: The claim is supported by participant data presented in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The recruited participants were relatively tall to increase the chances of successfully securing the tendon tapper device over a longer PT.
source: The recruited participants were relatively tall to increase the chances of successfully securing the tendon tapper device over a longer PT.
evidence: The claim explains the rationale for the participant selection criteria.

claim: Pilot testing revealed that individuals should be at least 181 cm tall for the study.
source: As pilot testing revealed that individuals should be at least 181 cm, we tested males only because we were not able to recruit any female participants that were this tall.
evidence: The claim is based on pilot testing data that informed the study design.

claim: Only males were tested because no female participants could be recruited that were at least 181 cm tall.
source: As pilot testing revealed that individuals should be at least 181 cm, we tested males only because we were not able to recruit any female participants that were this tall.
evidence: The claim explains the rationale for testing only male participants.

claim: All participants were free of knee injuries and neuromuscular disorders.
source: All participants were free of knee injuries and neuromuscular disorders.
evidence: The claim describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the local Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Sport Science at Ruhr University Bochum and conformed with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the local Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Sport Science at Ruhr University Bochum and conformed with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical approval for the study.
